title: Hagar and Sarah
aka: the allegory of Hagar and Sarah
lead: The story of Abraham's two wives, one a slave from Egypt and one free, and the later readings of it: Jewish tradition on Hagar and Ishmael, Paul's allegory in Galatians 4:21-31, the Christian history of using it, and Hagar in Islam and in womanist theology.

sections.b: Sarah, barren, gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abraham so that she may 'be built into a family through her' (Genesis 16:1-4). Hagar conceives, Sarah treats her harshly, and Hagar runs to the wilderness, where a messenger of the LORD finds her and she names God 'the God who sees me' (Genesis 16:7-14). After Isaac is born, Sarah sees Ishmael 'laughing' and has Hagar and her son sent away. God hears the boy and opens Hagar's eyes to a well (Genesis 21:8-21).

Jewish teachers read Ishmael's 'laughing' as something worse (Genesis Rabbah 53:11) and Hagar as Pharaoh's daughter (Genesis Rabbah 45:1, reported). Paul reads the pair as two covenants (Galatians 4:21-31). In Islam, Hagar (Hajar) is Ishmael's mother and the model of trust, and the pilgrim's run between Safa and Marwa remembers her search for water. Delores Williams read her as a figure for African American women in the wilderness. Each reading chooses a part of the story.
